claims.text: Ultrasound shows thrombi by visualizing the venous lining, abnormal vein compressibility or, with Doppler, impaired venous flow; approximately 90% sensitive and 98% specific for lower extremity DVT
claims.quote: Ultrasound identifies thrombi by directly visualizing the venous lining and by demonstrating abnormal vein compressibility or, with Doppler flow studies, impaired venous flow. The test is approximately 90% sensitive and 98% specific for lower extremity DVT (5).

claims.text: No single protocol is best; one approach: estimate probability with the Wells score; low probability + negative D-dimer excludes DVT; high probability or a positive D-dimer → compression ultrasound
claims.quote: No single testing protocol is best; one approach is for clinicians to first estimate the probability of a DVT using a validated clinical prediction rule such as the Wells score (1). In patients with a low probability, a negative D-dimer is considered sufficient to exclude DVT and avoid further imaging (2, 3). In patients with a high probability estimated by the clinical prediction rule, or those with a positive D-dimer, compression ultrasound is used to diagnose (or exclude) DVT (4).

claims.text: D-dimer is highly sensitive (approximately 96%) but nonspecific (approximately 37%)
claims.quote: In contrast to compression ultrasound, D-dimer is highly sensitive (sensitivity approximately 96%) but nonspecific (specificity approximately 37%) (4).

claims.text: Causes Classically, Virchow triad: impaired blood flow (stasis), endothelial injury and hypercoagulability
claims.quote: Classically, thrombosis occurs due to a combination of impaired blood flow (stasis), endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability (Virchow triad).

claims.text: Wells risk factors: active cancer, immobilization of the leg (eg, casting, recent long-distance travel), surgery with immobility > 3 days within the past 4 weeks, previous DVT
claims.quote: Active cancer (treatment ongoing or given within the previous 6 months) | Immobilization of lower extremity (eg, due to paralysis, paresis, casting, or recent long-distance travel) | Surgery leading to immobility for > 3 days within the past 4 weeks | Previous DVT

claims.text: Cancer is a risk factor (approximately 1 to 5% of patients with cancer develop VTE annually), strongest for pancreatic, brain, hematologic, lung and ovarian cancers
claims.quote: Cancer is a risk factor for DVT, particularly in older patients and in patients with recurrent thrombosis. Among all patients with cancer, approximately 1 to 5% develop a venous thromboembolism (VTE) annually (1, 2, 3). The association is strongest for pancreatic, brain, hematologic, lung, and ovarian cancers (2, 4).

claims.text: Symptoms Symptoms are nonspecific (vague aching, tenderness along the veins, edema, erythema); tenderness, whole-leg swelling, > 3 cm calf circumference difference, pitting edema and collateral superficial veins may be most specific; DVT is likely with ≥ 3 of these absent another likely diagnosis
claims.quote: When present, symptoms and signs of DVT (eg, vague aching pain, tenderness along the distribution of the veins, edema, erythema) are nonspecific, vary in frequency and severity, and are similar in arms and legs. Dilated collateral superficial veins may become visible or palpable. Calf discomfort elicited by ankle dorsiflexion with the knee extended (Homans sign) occasionally occurs with distal leg DVT but is neither sensitive nor specific. Tenderness, swelling of the whole leg, > 3 cm difference in circumference between calves, pitting edema, and collateral superficial veins may be most specific; DVT is likely with a combination of ≥ 3 in the absence of another likely diagnosis (see table ).

claims.text: In high-risk hospitalized patients DVT is often asymptomatic
claims.quote: Among patients who are hospitalized and are at high risk, deep vein thrombosis is often asymptomatic since typical features of swelling, redness, and tenderness may be less prominent in recumbent than ambulatory patients.

claims.text: Approximately 50% of patients with DVT have occult pulmonary emboli
claims.quote: Approximately 50% of patients with DVT have occult pulmonary emboli.

claims.text: Treatment and next step Her chart: anticoagulation

claims.text: Almost all patients get anticoagulants; the exception is isolated distal thrombi without severe symptoms (serial imaging, anticoagulate only if it extends)
claims.quote: Almost all patients with DVT are treated with anticoagulants (3, 4). The exception is patients with isolated distal thrombi without severe symptoms, in whom serial imaging and anticoagulation are needed only if the thrombus extends.

claims.text: DOACs (apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban, rivaroxaban) are preferred over warfarin as first-line treatment for DVT and PE, including cancer-associated thromboses
claims.quote: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOAC), including apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban, and rivaroxaban, are preferred over warfarin as first-line treatment for DVT and PE, including cancer-associated thromboses.

claims.text: Edoxaban or dabigatran start after 5 days of injectable heparin; rivaroxaban or apixaban may start immediately without heparin
claims.quote: For patients who are to start edoxaban (an oral factor Xa inhibitor) or dabigatran (an oral direct thrombin inhibitor), the oral agent is started after 5 days of injectable heparin (7). Alternatively, selected direct oral anticoagulants (rivaroxaban or apixaban) may be initiated immediately without first giving an injectable heparin.

claims.text: Initial duration 3 to 6 months; transient risk factors → can usually stop after 3 to 6 months; unprovoked or recurrent DVT, or a persistent risk factor (cancer, hypercoagulable state) → continue indefinitely with periodic re-evaluation
claims.quote: The initial duration of anticoagulation is 3 to 6 months (3, 4). Patients with transient risk factors for DVT (eg, immobilization, surgery) can usually discontinue anticoagulation after 3 to 6 months. Patients with idiopathic (or unprovoked) DVT with no known risk factors, recurrent DVT, or DVT due to a chronic and persistent risk factor (including cancer and hypercoagulable states such as antiphospholipid syndrome or protein C, protein S, or antithrombin deficiency) should continue anticoagulation indefinitely (extended anticoagulation) for secondary prevention of recurrent DVT and prevention of PE, with periodic re-evaluation of risks and benefits.

claims.text: An IVC filter may help prevent PE in lower extremity DVT when anticoagulation is contraindicated
claims.quote: An IVC filter may help prevent PE in patients with lower extremity DVT who have contraindications to anticoagulant therapy (3, 4).
